analysis.one_liner: Taxes ozone-depleting chemicals like CFCs and steers half the revenue into developing safer alternatives.
analysis.headline: Sen. Al Gore's bill to tax ozone-depleting chemicals was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have placed an excise tax, starting at $1 per pound in 1990 and rising to $5 by 1994 and adjusted for inflation, on the sale or import of chemicals known to destroy the stratospheric ozone layer, including common refrigerants like CFC-11 and CFC-12, and on imported goods made with them. Half of the money collected would go into a new Ozone Layer Conservation Trust Fund, which the EPA would use to plan and pay for research and development of replacement chemicals and technologies, including refrigeration and air-conditioning equipment suitable for export to developing countries. Chemicals recovered through recycling would be exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone exposed to UV radiation through a protected ozone layer, since the tax makes ozone-destroying chemicals more expensive and speeds the shift to replacements. American manufacturers of alternative refrigeration and air-conditioning equipment would also gain from federal block purchases, procurement preferences, and export assistance funded by the bill.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public and makers of replacement chemicals

how_it_helps.text: The tax starts at $1 per pound in 1990, rises to $5 per pound by 1994 with inflation adjustments, and is scaled by each chemical's ozone-depletion potential, so the worst chemicals like halon-1301 are taxed over 11 times harder than CFC-11.

Fifty percent of the tax revenue is appropriated to a new Ozone Layer Conservation Trust Fund, and the EPA must deliver a strategic plan within six months of enactment for using it to develop non-ozone-depleting alternatives.

The bill directs federal block purchases of ozone-safe refrigeration and air-conditioning equipment every 18 to 24 months with rising performance standards, preferential treatment in federal procurement, and help for U.S. manufacturers exporting that equipment to the developing world.
Chemicals diverted or recovered through recycling are exempt from the tax, rewarding recovery over new production.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers, producers, and importers of ozone-depleting chemicals pay the tax directly, and dealers owe a one-time floor-stocks tax on inventory held on January 1, 1990. The cost would largely be passed through to consumers in the prices of refrigerators, air conditioners, aerosol products, foams, and electronics made with these chemicals.
analysis.who_pays_short: Chemical makers and buyers of their products

drawbacks.text: The tax is ultimately paid by consumers, through higher prices on air conditioning, refrigeration, aerosols, foam products, and electronics that depend on these chemicals, a cost that falls hardest on households in hot climates buying cooling equipment.
Dealers holding inventories of the chemicals on January 1, 1990 owe a one-time floor stocks tax due by February 14, 1990, a cash hit on wholesalers and retailers.

Ozone depletion is a global problem, and a unilateral U.S. tax cannot by itself protect the layer; the bill addresses this only indirectly by funding alternatives suitable for developing countries, where use of these chemicals was growing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tax is a well-designed user fee: it charges the chemicals in proportion to the damage they do, exempts recycled material, and recycles half the revenue into developing replacements, which softens the transition. The main cost is modestly higher prices for cooling and related goods during the phase-in. For a pollutant linked to skin cancer and ecosystem damage, the trade-off favors the tax.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Sen. Albert Gore Jr. introduced the Ozone Layer Conservation Act of 1989 on May 1, 1989, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action was ever taken: the bill received no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no House counterpart action appears in its history.
One senator, a Democrat, cosponsored the bill, giving it two supporters out of 100 senators.

The bill would have taxed a list of eleven ozone-depleting chemicals including CFCs, carbon tetrachloride, methyl chloroform, and halons, with rates rising from $1 per pound in 1990 to $5 per pound in 1994.
Half the revenue was to fund an Ozone Layer Conservation Trust Fund for EPA-planned development of replacement technologies, including federal block purchases of ozone-safe refrigeration equipment.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers and importers of ozone-depleting chemicals were better off, since no excise tax took effect from this bill, and buyers of CFC-dependent products avoided the price increases. The public got no protection from this bill; the effort died quietly in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Chemical producers; the bill died untouched

for.name: Sen. Albert Gore, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate on May 1, 1989.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

against.name: Sen. Lloyd Bentsen
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that never acted on the bill, leaving it to die without consideration.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and both known supporters were Democrats, so the partisan shape of any hypothetical floor fight is unknown.

industries.note: The bill taxes every pound of CFCs, halons, carbon tetrachloride, methyl chloroform, and methylene chloride they sell or import, plus goods made with them, directly shrinking their main product market. Their interest in avoiding the tax ran against the public's interest in a protected ozone layer.

They would face higher input costs as CFC prices rose, but the trust fund would finance development of non-ozone-depleting equipment, and the bill mandates federal block purchases, procurement preferences, and export assistance that would create an early market for exactly their replacement products.
Recovered and diverted chemicals are explicitly exempt from the tax, making recycled refrigerant cheaper than newly manufactured chemical and rewarding recovery businesses.

Imported goods made with ozone-depleting chemicals are taxed, and the de minimis exemption is unavailable for products using these chemicals in refrigeration, air conditioning, aerosols, foams, or electronics production, raising their costs.
